paras: The shooting of Hicks by Constable King took place in Sampson County, North Carolina, in late November 1882, when a constable serving an arrest warrant seriously wounded Hicks, a Black schoolteacher. The only surviving report, a brief item from the Clinton Caucasian reprinted in Raleigh, said that Hicks had resisted the officer with an axe.

Hicks, described as a "negro" schoolteacher, had been released from the county jail only a few days before the shooting. Constable King of Piney Grove Township then obtained a warrant for his arrest, though the charge is not given in the coverage.

According to the Caucasian, King was proceeding to execute the warrant when Hicks, "not wishing to be again confined in the county jail," resisted him with an axe. King shot Hicks, and the paper said only that he was "seriously" wounded. The item does not say where the shooting took place, at what time, or whether anyone else was present.
No report of Hicks's recovery or death, of an inquiry into the shooting, or of the outcome of the warrant against him was found.

The episode survives in a single paragraph that the Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic printed on December 6, 1882, credited to the Clinton Caucasian, among unrelated items on a Virginia obituary, railroad stock and election returns. The item called Hicks "the atrocious pedagogue" and explained the shooting entirely through his resistance, presenting the constable's version as fact. No account from Hicks or any witness other than the officer's side appears, and no other paper carrying the story was found.
